passage:
At their school in Osaka, Hana had found a way to make the whole class laugh: copying the careful, slow way Jin read aloud. Every time she did it, the back row cheered, and Hana felt powerful, like the star of a show.
By the third week, though, something changed. When teams were picked for the science project, nobody picked Hana. At lunch, the same kids who had cheered talked about her in low voices. One girl said, "She's funny, but I wouldn't trust her."
Hana stared at her rice. The cheering had felt so big. Now it felt like nothing.
The next time Jin read aloud, Hana kept quiet. Afterwards she said, "Your reading was good today, Jin."

qa.q: What did Hana copy to make the class laugh?
qa.a: The careful, slow way Jin read aloud.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when nobody picked her for the science project?
qa.a: She felt hurt and empty, realising the cheering had not turned into real respect.

qa.q: What did Hana choose instead of more mocking, and why was it wiser?
qa.a: She stayed quiet and complimented Jin, choosing respect over thin applause that had already faded.

qa.q: How might the girl who said she wouldn't trust Hana see her?
qa.a: The girl sees Hana as entertaining but unkind, someone who might turn the jokes on anyone.

grounding: A girl feels powerful when classmates cheer her mockery, but the applause fades and they do not respect her, so she stops and chooses respect.

At the dance academy, Alka liked to copy Ishita's wobbly turns during water breaks. The other girls clapped and squealed. Alka took a bow each time.
But on the evening of the class show, Alka forgot her steps on stage. Afterwards, in the changing room, she waited for the girls to comfort her. Nobody came. They were all around Ishita, helping her with her hairpins.
Alka heard one of them whisper, "Now she knows how it feels."
Her face burned. The clapping had never really been for her.
The next practice, when Ishita wobbled, Alka didn't copy her. She said, "Try leaning a bit forward. It helped me."

qa.q: Where did Alka copy Ishita's turns?
qa.a: At the dance academy, during water breaks.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when nobody came to comfort her?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and alone, realising the girls who clapped had not really been on her side.

qa.q: What did Alka do differently at the next practice?
qa.a: Instead of mocking Ishita, she offered a helpful tip, choosing respect over applause.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Alka gives her the tip?
qa.a: Ishita may feel surprised and a little wary, but also relieved to be helped instead of mocked.

grounding: A girl enjoys her classmates clapping when she mocks another dancer, then sees they do not respect her, and chooses to help instead.

At the weekly haat near their village, three older boys were pushing Bablu, the potter's son, from one to the other, laughing as his clay cups smashed.
Arnab felt his chest ache. He couldn't fight three older boys. But he couldn't walk away either.
He grabbed Alka's hand. "Come on." They walked straight to Bablu, and Arnab said, loud and clear, "Leave him."
The boys hesitated. A shopkeeper looked over. They drifted away.
Arnab and Alka helped Bablu pick up the pieces. Then they went to the headmaster's house by the temple and told him. The headmaster thanked them and said he'd speak to the boys' families that evening.

qa.q: What was Bablu carrying that got smashed?
qa.a: Clay cups.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he saw Bablu being pushed?
qa.a: He felt compassion, with an ache in his chest, and couldn't bear to walk away.

qa.q: Which small actions helped Bablu?
qa.a: Walking to him with Alka, saying "Leave him", helping pick up the pieces and telling the headmaster that same day.

qa.q: How might Bablu have felt when Arnab and Alka came over?
qa.a: Bablu probably felt less alone and relieved that someone stood up for him.

Felix watched from the bench. His stomach twisted. He felt sorry for him, but what could he do?
Then he remembered that small things count. He walked over and sat on the wall next to Abebe. "Do you want to play with us instead?" he asked, pointing to his friends.
Abebe nodded. The older boys went off to find someone else.
After the break, Felix told Frau Weber what he'd seen. She thanked him and said she'd watch the yard herself tomorrow.

Counsellor's note, Wednesday.
Akash came to my room during the last period, very quiet. He said that on Monday, two Class 7 boys trapped Tushar in the washroom and took his lunch money. Akash had been there but said nothing.
"If I'd spoken, they'd have come for me next," he said. His hands were twisting in his lap.

passage:
At the badminton club, Jeevan watched two older players knock Sonu's racket out of his hand again and again, laughing. Jeevan kept his eyes on his own shuttle and said nothing.
On the way home, his cycle felt heavy. He kept seeing Sonu's face. He felt terrible. He could have done something.

Sonu shrugged, but his eyes were grateful.
Then Jeevan went to Coach Sabina. She listened and said she'd move Sonu to her own court and talk to the older players before practice.

"Bhupen, your Ujjwal Dada once laughed at something he shouldn't have. I was twelve. A boy in our class, Moti, stammered when he read aloud. The class leader started copying him, and everyone laughed, so I laughed too. I didn't want to be the odd one out.

It wasn't a big speech. We just stopped. And the leader stopped too, because nobody was laughing."

grounding: A grandfather recalls laughing along to fit in, seeing it make the teaser bolder, then refusing to laugh, which others copied until the teasing stopped.

I'm Vidya, and in Class 5 I saw something I couldn't forget. Behind the library, two boys took Vaibhav's lunch box and ate his food while he watched, silent.
I thought about it all afternoon. If I told, would everyone call me a snitch?

Vinita turned back to her sandwich. Not my problem, she told herself. Someone else will say something.
